name: Menya
confidence_why: The only first-hand description, Whitehead's 2004 reference grammar (repeating his 1992 SIL phonology statement word for word), says stress falls on the last or second-last syllable with tone and stress interdependent and tone possibly phonemic, so the placement is genuinely unfixed rather than merely unrecorded, and Lloyd's 1973 family survey agrees that Angan tone and stress form one complex unit; nothing contradicts this, but it all rests on one fieldworker.
catalog_citation: Whitehead, Carl R. 2004. A reference grammar of Menya, an Angan language of Papua New Guinea. PhD thesis, University of Manitoba, ix+265 pp. (MSpace hdl 1993/17921, scanned); March 2006 web-version, Ukarumpa: SIL-PNG Academic Publications, 277 pp. (SIL archive 9799). Same statement in Whitehead, Carl. 1992 (updated Sept. 1999). Menya Organised Phonology Data. Ukarumpa: SIL-PNG, 4 pp. (SIL archive 42434), p. 3.
catalog_locator: Appendix A 'Organized phonology data statement', subsection 'Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length)', p. 226 (2004 scan: read; 2006 web-version: p. 238; Whitehead 1992/1999 OPD: p. 3)
catalog_quote: Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length) The norm is for stress to be on the ultimate or penultimate syllable. Words of more than three syllables usually have two stressed syllables with the latter being the stronger. Tone and stress are inter-dependent. Tone might be phonemic, but the functional load is low.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls at the right edge, on either the final or the penultimate syllable (the source does not say what decides between them); primary stress is the rightmost stress. Tone interacts with stress and may be marginally phonemic.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Words of more than three syllables usually carry two stresses, the later (rightmost) one being the stronger, i.e. a weaker secondary stress earlier in the word; its position is not specified.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated as exceptions. Elsewhere in the grammar: compound noun stems merge into one word with a single stress (e.g. stress only on the second syllable of a two-root compound, 3.2.2.1 p. 42) whereas compound NP heads keep one stress per noun (3.3.1.1 p. 48); clitics 'bear no stress' and particles are 'not normally stressed' (glossary p. 261).
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is about the (phonological) word in an SIL Organised Phonology Data format; the grammar adds that adjunct-noun + verb phrases form one phonological unit with the verb bearing the phrasal stress (p. 145). No acoustic evidence; author flags possible low-load phonemic tone.
new_statements.identity_note: Whitehead's description is based on the village of Akwanja (Northeast sociolect group, 9 km ENE of Menyamya); he states the study 'pertains primarily to the Northeast dialect' of Menya (2004/2006 p. 7). NB: Glottolog ref 693320 'Gao, Yang 2015, Description du menya, EHESS' is misassigned to this language: theses.fr record 2015EHES0181 ('Description de la langue Menya : phonologie et syntaxe', dir. L. Sagart & G. Jacques) has subject 'Muya (langue de Chine)', Tibeto-Burman, i.e. the Qiangic language Muya/Minyak of Sichuan, not Angan Menya.

sources.note: Identical Appendix A statement p. 226 (ultimate or penultimate; two stresses in words >3 syllables, latter stronger; tone/stress inter-dependent). Body adds: compound noun stems carry a single stress, e.g. only on the second syllable (3.2.2.1, p. 42) whereas compound NP heads keep separate word stresses (3.3.1.1, p. 48); in adjunct+verb phrases the verb bears the phrasal stress (p. 145); glossary p. 261: clitics bear no stress, particles are not normally stressed.

sources.note: p. 3 'Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length)': same wording as the grammar appendix (with typo 'stornger'): stress normally ultimate or penultimate; >3-syllable words usually have two stresses, the latter stronger; tone and stress inter-dependent; tone might be phonemic, functional load low.
